source: Rabanser et al. (2026) Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability
finding: Twelve metrics in four dimensions (consistency, robustness, predictability, safety), taken from safety-critical engineering, were applied to 15 models on two agent benchmarks. Capability gains over about 24 months brought only small reliability gains.
numbers: 15 models, 2 benchmarks (tau-bench, GAIA), 12 metrics. Fault injection at p_fault=0.2; 5 paraphrases per task; medium-intensity tool-format changes. Reliability gain small; tau-bench moderate, GAIA barely any.
limits: Only a subset of real environment shifts tested. Authors say benchmark difficulty and protocol may also explain the trend. LLM judge used for severity.
agent_relevance: Accuracy alone hides brittleness. Our agent should report run-to-run consistency and perturbation drop, not one accuracy number.

source: Rabanser et al. (2026) Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability
finding: Robustness is uneven. Models handled injected tool faults and tool-format changes well (ceiling effects) but remained sensitive to harmless paraphrasing of the instruction.
numbers: Fault and environment robustness near ceiling for most models; prompt robustness was the main differentiator across models. Robustness not related to task difficulty.
quote: models handle genuine technical failures gracefully yet remain vulnerable to surface-level variations
limits: Ceiling effects mean the fault tests may be too easy. Paraphrases were generated by GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: Resilience to loud faults is not the same as resilience to quiet wording changes. The schema should include a rephrase-and-recheck step for the task statement.

source: Rabanser et al. (2026) Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability
finding: Agents that can solve a task often fail to solve it consistently. Action types are repeatable ('what') but action order is not ('when').
numbers: Outcome consistency stayed low across all 15 models on both benchmarks (values roughly 0.52 to 0.86 in the figure). Distribution consistency was higher than sequence consistency.
limits: Values read off a garbled figure; exact per-model numbers need the paper tables.
agent_relevance: Single-run success overstates ability. A second independent pass or a vote is a cheap monitor for the 'monitor' potential.

source: Rabanser et al. (2026) Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability
finding: Calibration of self-reported confidence improved in recent models (Claude models named as strongest), but discrimination did not improve on the open-ended GAIA benchmark.
numbers: Confidence taken by post-hoc self-assessment after the run. Calibration improved; GAIA discrimination flat or worse in some recent models.
limits: Self-rating after the fact; single prompt format.
agent_relevance: Confidence can be a weak monitoring signal but should not be the only trigger for a look-back.

source: Yao et al. (2024) tau-bench: a benchmark for tool-agent-user interaction
finding: Introduced pass^k, the chance that all k repeated trials of the same task succeed. Strong function-calling agents were inconsistent: pass^8 fell far below pass^1.
numbers: gpt-4o retail pass^1 about 61.2 and airline about 35.2; pass^8 below 25% on retail. Overall under 50% task success.
limits: Simulated users (LLM); two domains; 2024 models.
agent_relevance: pass^k is a ready reliability measure for a scaffold: does the schema raise pass^k, not just pass@1.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
finding: MAST taxonomy of 14 failure modes in 3 clusters, built from 150 traces and applied to 1600+ traces over 7 frameworks. Clusters: system design 41.8%, inter-agent misalignment 36.9%, task verification 21.3%.
numbers: Inter-annotator kappa 0.88 on the final human round; LLM judge kappa 0.77 vs humans. Modes include step repetition (15.7%), not recognising task completion (12.4%), reasoning-action mismatch (13.2%), proceeding on wrong assumption (6.8%).
limits: Percentages are from the paper text for the full dataset; some figure values differ slightly between versions. Frameworks and tasks are 2024-25 era.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM analogue of Woods's patterns: step repetition fits 'stuck in outdated behaviour'; ignored input and derailment fit 'working at cross purposes'.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
finding: Targeted interventions on diagnosed failures raised success. Better role specifications alone gave +9.4% for ChatDev (same model GPT-4o). Adding a high-level task verification step gave +15.6% on ProgramDev.
numbers: Success-rate gains +9.4% and +15.6%; small human-checked sets (about 30 traces for some systems).
limits: Authors say inter-agent misalignment needs deeper fixes (social reasoning), not only protocol changes.
agent_relevance: A cheap verification gate against the original goal is a tested look-back with a measured size.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: Across 6 tasks and 200,000+ simulated conversations, top LLMs scored 39% lower on average when the instruction arrived in pieces over turns. Most of the loss was unreliability, not lost aptitude.
numbers: Average drop 39%. Best-case (aptitude) loss about 15%; unreliability up about 112% in the headline plot. CONCAT baseline kept 95.1% of FULL, so the loss is not missing information.
quote: when LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover
limits: Simulated user with sharded instructions; generation tasks only. Temperature 1 default.
agent_relevance: This is the 'stuck in outdated behaviour' pattern: the model commits to an early assumption and does not revise. Supports a scheduled 'reopen early assumptions' step.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: Agent-style mitigation only partly helped. Restating all instructions in a final turn (RECAP) or every turn (SNOWBALL) improved results but stayed below the single-turn level. Lowering temperature to 0 did not fix it.
numbers: RECAP beat SNOWBALL; both below FULL/CONCAT. With assistant and user temperature at 0, GPT-4o-mini showed no reliability gain in sharded runs; GPT-4o gained about 15-20%. In FULL/CONCAT, unreliability fell 50-80% at lower temperature.
limits: RECAP needs to know the last turn in advance, so it is unrealistic. Tested on GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini only.
agent_relevance: A recap of the original goal helps a bit but is not a cure. Look-back must also rewrite or discard stale commitments.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without outside feedback, asking the model to review and fix its own answer did not help and often hurt. Earlier gains came from oracle labels.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA fell from 75.8 to 38.1 after one self-correct round (41.8 after two). GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 and 74.7. On GSM8K GPT-3.5 kept its first answer 74.7% of the time. Llama-2 GSM8K 62.0 to 43.5 and 36.5.
limits: Models are GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2 (2023); prompts from earlier papers; newer reasoning models may differ.
agent_relevance: An unaided look-back can damage correct answers. Look-back should use external checks (tests, tools, independent sample), not only self-review.

source: Moerman et al. (2022) Graceful extensibility in asset management (railway case)
finding: A single longitudinal case (V250 high-speed train introduction, 11+ years) was coded against Woods's 10 proto-theorems of graceful extensibility. Most predicted patterns were matched.
numbers: 176 coded items; 24 sub-patterns; 21 matched, 3 not fully observed. 31% of coded items on saturation risk (S1-S3), 46% on networks of adaptive units (S4-S6), 23% on outmanoeuvring constraints (S7-S10). No evidence for the base vs extended capacity distinction (S7.1).
limits: One case, pattern-matching by the authors, theory-confirming design. Authors say no conclusions can be drawn from the coded-item shares.
agent_relevance: The theory is testable and partly supported in the field, but only by case studies. Treat the potentials and failure patterns as a checklist, not a verified model.

source: Iflaifel et al. (2020) Resilient Health Care: a systematic review of conceptualisations, study methods and factors
finding: Systematic review of resilient health care. Descriptions were consistent (adjust before, during or after events), but methods were mostly qualitative and no intervention effects were measured.
numbers: 872 records, 74 full texts, 36 included (20 journal, 16 book). Five studies built on Hollnagel's four capabilities. Factors named: team relationships, trade-offs, resilience training.
limits: Thematic synthesis; mixed quality; authors say a gold-standard method is not yet identified and interventions still need testing.
agent_relevance: No effect sizes exist for training for resilience. We cannot import numbers; we must test the agent version ourselves.

source: Cooper (2022) The Emperor has no clothes: a critique of Safety-II
finding: A critique paper says the Resilience Engineering / Safety-II / HOP ideas are untested propositions with no peer-reviewed empirical proof that they improve safety or cut injuries.
numbers: No data analysis. Claim: no published peer-reviewed experimental evidence; proposes field experiments on injury rates.
quote: no published, peer-reviewed empirical evidence demonstrates whether or not any aspect of New-View's propositions are valid
limits: A position paper by a Safety-1 advocate; occupational-safety focus (injuries), not complex-system anomalies. Contested by RE scholars.
agent_relevance: Honest control: the theory has concepts and case evidence but not trial evidence. Do not oversell.

source: Herrera, Praetorius, Degerman, Wiig (2025) Resilience Engineering: theoretical and practical reflections on a 20-year journey
finding: A critical 20-year overview. Resilience moved from 'a property' (2004) to 'a verb' (2024), and the term spread widely. Empirical work only began about 2015. Authors call for solid evidence that management measures improve work as done.
numbers: Empirical RE research emerged around 2015; healthcare tools well received in Norway and Sweden; maritime applications remain 'an exercise for a limited group of researchers'.
limits: A reflective paper, not a systematic review. Authors note growing confusion between Safety-II and resilience.
agent_relevance: The four potentials are used loosely. Define them operationally for the agent instead of relying on the field's definitions.

source: Or (2025) MTTR-A: measuring cognitive recovery latency in multi-agent systems
finding: Proposes a recovery-time metric for LLM multi-agent runs after reasoning drift, with reflex types (auto-replan, tool-retry, rollback, human-approve).
numbers: 200 LangGraph runs; median recovery 6.21 s (SD 2.14, p90 10.73 s). Auto-replan 5.94 s (n=93), tool-retry 4.46 s (n=42), rollback 6.99 s (n=44), human-approve 12.22 s. About 8% of runtime spent recovering.
limits: Semi-simulated: synthetic corpus, controlled reflex latencies, AG News retrieval. It measures speed, not whether the recovery was correct.
agent_relevance: A usable 'respond' metric, but needs real drift traces and a correctness check before it means anything.

source: Xiao, Sun, Chen (2026) AIR: Improving Agent Safety through Incident Response
finding: An incident-response loop (detect, contain/recover, then write guardrail rules) built into the agent loop. Detection, remediation and eradication were all above 90% in the authors' tests.
numbers: Remediation ablation: embodied agent 92.3% to 80.95% without rule-specified remediation; computer-use agent 97.7% to 76.6%. Over 3 rounds incidents fell 54 to 6 to 0 (code), 67 to 5 to 2 (embodied), 8 to 1 to 0 (computer use). Guardrails converged to 9, 11, 6 rules. No false positives on safe embodied tasks; computer-use agent finished only 8 of 35 safe tasks.
limits: Authors' own incident sets; no external baselines exist; rules tested on the same task distribution they were learned from.
agent_relevance: Shows the 'learn' potential can be coded: turn each incident into a rule. Risk of overfitting to seen incidents.

source: Liu et al. (2026) Resilience Matters for Embodied Agents System
finding: Maps Woods's four capabilities (rebound, robustness, graceful extensibility, sustained adaptability) to metrics for embodied LLM agents. Success rate hides large differences in recovery cost.
numbers: Habitat-Sim, 400 household tasks, 10 methods. Reflexion vs CoPAL success 56.3% vs 55.8% but recovery cost differs 4.8 times. Physical perturbation raised recovery cost from 11.6 to 36.3; stress and recovery cost correlated, Spearman 0.82.
limits: Simulated household tasks; metric weights set by the authors; preprint.
agent_relevance: Two agents with equal accuracy can differ a lot in how they recover. Measure recovery cost, not only success.

source: Liu et al. (2026) Resilience Matters for Embodied Agents System
finding: Metric-guided fixes cut recovery effort. A feedback-guided recovery layer and a consistency record for replanning reduced oscillation and repeated subtasks.
numbers: Recovery cost 59.11 to 33.73; recovery window 3.13 to 2.38. Replanning step variance 0.3185 to 0.2552. Trade-off: optimising graceful extensibility raised recovery cost.
limits: Single environment; one optimisation per metric; trade-offs across resilience aspects.
agent_relevance: A 'consistency record' of completed subtasks and recent actions directly targets repeat-loop behaviour.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) ResMAS: Resilience Optimization in LLM-based Multi-agent Systems
finding: Under random agent failures at error rates 0 to 1, a group of agents was more resilient than one agent. Resilience rose with the number of agents and links. Topology and prompt design each changed resilience.
numbers: Resilience = area under accuracy-vs-error-rate curve, tested at p=0, .2, .4, .6, .8, 1; 7936 topology-task-correctness tuples for the reward model; ResMAS beat G-Designer, OPRO, TextGrad, GPTSwarm baselines on MATH, MMLU-Pro and Chess.
limits: Failures injected at random, not realistic cognitive failures. More agents costs more. Table values garbled in PDF text, so exact gains not recorded.
agent_relevance: Redundancy raises resilience but costs compute. Also more agents means more coordination failures (see MAST).

source: Yu, Bentley, Carroll (2026) Operational Hallucination and Safety Drift in AI Agents
finding: Reports repeated identical tool calls (livelock) and refusals in text followed by unsafe actions in multi-turn agent loops, across 7 models.
numbers: Livelock flag = 3 or more identical consecutive tool calls; turns capped at 10. Dataset only 4 scenarios. Text-action gap +1.00 for several models in the malicious case (single episode per model).
limits: Tiny sample, single episodes, deterministic replay. Fractions such as 0, 0.5, 1 are not statistics.
agent_relevance: Gives a cheap stuck-loop detector (3 identical calls). Evidence is weak; treat as a hypothesis.

source: Woods and Branlat (2011) Basic patterns in how adaptive systems fail
finding: Names three basic patterns: decompensation (capacity to adapt runs out as problems cascade), working at cross purposes (locally adaptive, globally maladaptive) and getting stuck in outdated behaviours. Derived from healthcare, mission control, military and firefighting studies.
numbers: No quantitative effect sizes found in the secondary text seen (search summary only).
limits: Chapter not opened (publisher page returned 403); only a search summary was read. Patterns are descriptive, not tested by experiment.
agent_relevance: Source for the three failure patterns we map to impasse detection. No numbers to carry over.

source: Woods et al. (2014) EUROCONTROL: Patterns in How People Think and Work
finding: Pattern-centred inquiry report. Lists recurring patterns from the Columbia accident, including failure to revise assessments as new evidence accumulates and taking past success as a reason for confidence.
numbers: Five recurring patterns in Table 1 (drift toward failure; past success as confidence; fragmented problem solving; failure to revise assessments; breakdowns at unit boundaries). Qualitative.
limits: Case-based; patterns are post-hoc from accident reports; hindsight bias risk; no controlled test.
agent_relevance: Pattern 4 (failure to revise assessments) is the human match for the LLM 'lost in conversation' result. Basis for a revise-on-new-evidence rule.

source: Synthesis across Rabanser (2026), Laban (2025), Cemri (2025), tau-bench (2024)
finding: Four independent LLM studies agree that success on one clean run says little about robust behaviour. Failures are inconsistency, stale assumptions and weak verification, not missing capability.
numbers: Consistency low (Rabanser); 39% multi-turn drop (Laban); verification gaps 21.3% of failures (Cemri); pass^8 below 25% (tau-bench).
limits: Different tasks, models and metrics; cannot be pooled into one effect size. No LLM study found that tests Woods's framework directly as an intervention.
agent_relevance: Gap: no direct LLM test of the four potentials. Our schema's look-back would be a first test.

source: Rabanser et al. (2026) Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability
finding: Safety analysis on tau-bench: the newest frontier models had clearly fewer rule violations, and wrong charges or refunds stayed the most common violation for all models.
numbers: Four constraint types checked over multi-turn customer-service runs; violations stratified by severity; frontier models lower overall.
limits: Violations judged by an LLM; one domain.
agent_relevance: Bounded error size is a separate property from accuracy; add a pre-commit check on irreversible steps.

source: Xiao, Sun, Chen (2026) AIR: Improving Agent Safety through Incident Response
finding: Authors state no direct baselines exist for incident response in LLM agents, and generated guardrails can be too broad (false positives) or too narrow (miss other hazards).
numbers: Rule quality in the paper: embodied rules about 95.97% and 88.8% on two measures in Table 6 (values read from garbled table).
limits: No external comparison; table values partly unclear.
agent_relevance: Learned rules need a precision check, or they will block good work.
